warmup.q: transfer() is synchronized and moves money between two balances. total() adds the balances and is not synchronized. Can total() return a wrong number while transfers run?
options: No, because transfer() is synchronized, so it is atomic for everyone
Yes, because total() does not take the lock, so it can read between the debit and the credit
Only on machines with more than one core
No, because reading a long is atomic
warmup.why: A lock only keeps out threads that ask for the same lock. total() walks straight past it and can read after the debit but before the credit. Reading one long may be atomic, but reading two of them is still two steps. Readers need the lock as much as writers do, and the first section measures how often the unlocked reader gets it wrong.

opening:
Race conditions: why count++ lies ended on a job that no single call can do: a transfer. It debits one balance and credits another, and nobody may see the money in flight. The usual answer is one word, synchronized, added to the transfer method.

That's a fair instinct. The keyword is built into the language, it has been there since Java 1.0, and for the transfer itself it works.

The catch is in what the word promises, and to whom.

Picture the nightly audit that adds up every balance while transfers keep running. The transfer method is synchronized. The audit isn't, because it only reads, and reading never hurt anyone. Some audits come out short by exactly the amount in flight, while the transfer code is perfect.

In this lesson, we'll put the transfer under a lock and see what synchronized guarantees, and to whom. Then we'll choose the object to lock on, and keep slow and foreign code out of the locked region. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with an audit that came up short while the transfer code was perfect. The lock had kept its promise to every thread that asked for the key, and the auditor never asked. Then we let a thread back into its own lock, chose a key nobody can borrow, and moved the issuer call out of the room.

Now search your own code for synchronized and read what runs inside each block. A call to Oracle, the card issuer or a listener in there is a queue waiting for traffic.

Next, we'll answer the question this lesson left open: how can a thread wait inside a lock for the next payment to arrive, without keeping the key while it waits?

sections.h: Locking the transfer: what synchronized promises, and to whom
sections.html:
We'll start where the last lesson stopped. Left alone, a transfer is two read-modify-writes in a row, and we know what eight threads do to those. So let's make the pair one step. Every Java object carries a built-in lock, and synchronized takes it on the way in and gives it back on the way out:

Java
private final Object lock = new Object();
private long a = 100, b = 100;       // two balances, in cents

void transfer(long cents) {
    synchronized (lock) {        // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free
        a -= cents;
        b += cents;
    }                            // give it back, even if the block throws
}
Kotlin
private val lock = Any()
private var a = 100L                 // two balances, in cents
private var b = 100L

fun transfer(cents: Long) {
    synchronized(lock) {         // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free
        a -= cents
        b += cents
    }                            // give it back, even if the block throws
}

Both versions say the same thing. In Java synchronized is a keyword, and in Kotlin it's a library function that the compiler turns into the same bytecode. javap shows it plainly: a monitorenter before the two lines, a monitorexit after them, and a second monitorexit on the path an exception takes.

The lock every object carries is called its monitor, or intrinsic lock.

Picture a room with one key. A thread takes the key and goes in. Every other thread that wants the same key waits in the corridor, in the BLOCKED state from A thread's life. Before leaving, the thread writes its results on the whiteboard, and the next thread to take the key reads them. The monitor is the key, and the room is the code that synchronized guards.

That picture holds both guarantees that synchronized gives you.

Mutual exclusion: while one thread holds a monitor, no other thread can enter a block guarded by the same monitor. So the debit and the credit happen as one step.

Visibility: everything a thread wrote before it released a monitor is visible to the next thread that takes the same monitor. The memory model calls that a happens-before edge from the release to the next lock.

A synchronized instance method is shorthand for synchronized (this) around the whole body. A static synchronized method locks the class object, such as Ledger.class.

Notice the words both guarantees share: the same monitor. The monitor is strict, and very literal. It keeps out every thread that asks for its key, and it pays no attention to threads that don't ask.

The warm-up's auditor is one of those threads. AuditDemo runs a transfer thread that moves 50 cents back and forth 200,000 times, always under the lock. Meanwhile an auditor adds up a + b as fast as it can. Both balances start at 1,000, so every audit should say 2,000.

Here are two runs, without and with the lock in the auditor:

auditor skipped the lock: 41,004,159 audits, 2,813,398 saw a total other than 2,000
auditor took the lock: 905,017 audits, 0 saw a total other than 2,000

The transfer was correct all along. Without the lock, about one audit in fifteen caught the 50 cents in flight, in neither account. With the lock, not one of 905,017 audits was wrong. The price shows in the other number: the locked auditor got through far fewer audits, because each one now waits its turn for the key.

A lock protects only the threads that take it. Readers take it too.

You can play the auditor by hand in the simulator. Step T1 halfway through its transfer, then let T2 read. Then try the same trick on T3.

Real classes have more than one synchronized method, though, and the methods call each other. So what happens when a thread that already holds the key asks for it again?

sim.title: A transfer under a lock, and two auditors
sim.intro: T1 moves 50 from a to b while holding the lock. T2 audits without the lock, T3 with it. Make T2 see a total of 150. Then try to make T3 see anything but 200.

try.title: Audit with and without the lock
steps: Read AuditDemo. A transfer thread moves 50 cents back and forth 200,000 times, always under the lock. The auditor adds a + b without it.
Run it with the command below and note how many audits were wrong.
Predict the count of wrong totals when the auditor takes the lock too. Then run it again with -Pargs=locked.

code.title: AuditDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. */ public class AuditDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); // volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent static volatile long a = 1_000, b = 1_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean auditorLocks = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Thread transfers = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { synchronized (lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50; b += 50; } synchronized (lock) { // and move it back a += 50; b -= 50; } } }); Thread auditor = new Thread(() -> { long audits = 0, wrong = 0; while (transfers.isAlive()) { long total; if (auditorLocks) { synchronized (lock) { total = a + b; } } else { total = a + b; // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++; if (total != 2_000) wrong++; } System.out.printf("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000%n", auditorLocks ? "took" : "skipped", audits, wrong); }); transfers.start(); auditor.start(); transfers.join(); auditor.join(); } }

alt.title: AuditDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. private val lock = Any() // @Volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent @Volatile private var a = 1_000L @Volatile private var b = 1_000L fun main(args: Array<String>) { val auditorLocks = args.firstOrNull() == "locked" val transfers = thread { repeat(200_000) { synchronized(lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50 b += 50 } synchronized(lock) { // and move it back a += 50 b -= 50 } } } val auditor = thread { var audits = 0L var wrong = 0L while (transfers.isAlive) { val total = if (auditorLocks) { synchronized(lock) { a + b } } else { a + b // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++ if (total != 2_000L) wrong++ } println("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000" .format(if (auditorLocks) "took" else "skipped", audits, wrong)) } transfers.join() auditor.join() }

try.expect: Without the lock, millions of audits see a total other than 2,000 (one run here: 2,813,398 of 41,004,159). With the lock, zero, every run, though the auditor gets through far fewer audits because it waits for the key. The writer was correct all along. The reader was the bug.

aside.title: The demo's balances are volatile. Why isn't that enough?
aside.html: volatile makes each read see the latest write to that one field, and that's why AuditDemo uses it: without it, the JIT could read the balances once and never again. But the auditor reads two fields, one after the other, and a transfer can run between the two reads. Each read is fresh, and the pair still doesn't match. To make two fields change together, you need a lock, or one immutable object that you swap in a single step, which lesson 8 of this track does with AtomicReference.

video.title: A monitor is a room with one key: one thread inside, the rest BLOCKED in the entry set, each unlock hands its writes to the next lock, and the owner can walk back in

sections.h: Calling one locked method from another: reentrancy
sections.html:
Here's that question in the ledger. An account's withdraw asks canCover before it takes the money, and both methods are synchronized on the same account:

Java
public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) {
    if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents;   // canCover takes the same lock
}

public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) {
    return balanceCents >= cents;
}
Kotlin
@Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) {
    if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents    // canCover takes the same lock
}

@Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean = balanceCents >= cents

This is the overdraft check from the last lesson, made safe. The check and the debit sit inside one locked method, so no other withdrawal can get in between. But look at what withdraw does while it holds the account's monitor: it calls canCover, which asks for that same monitor. If a thread had to wait for a key it already holds, it would wait forever.

It doesn't wait, because Java monitors are reentrant. A thread that holds a monitor can enter any block guarded by the same monitor without waiting. The JVM keeps a hold count for each monitor. Each entry adds one, each exit takes one away, and the monitor is free again at zero.

In the room picture, the thread with the key can walk back in through another door. In code, a synchronized method that calls another one on the same object never waits for itself.

Subclasses rely on the same rule. In ReentrancyDemo, an AuditedAccount overrides withdraw with a synchronized method that logs a line and calls super.withdraw, which then calls canCover. One thread enters one monitor three deep, and Thread.holdsLock(this) prints true at every level.

Reentrancy has a side effect worth knowing now, because the lab is built on it. The lock lets the same thread back in while your object is halfway through a change.

Say a synchronized method publish loops over its listeners, and one listener calls subscribe, which is synchronized too. The lock lets it straight in, because it's the same thread. subscribe adds to the list that publish is iterating, and the loop dies with ConcurrentModificationException.

The lock did its job. It was never meant to stop the thread that already holds it.

So far, every lock in this lesson has been an object we picked without much thought. Which object should hold the key, then? Any object can, and that's the trouble.

try.title: Enter the same lock three times
steps: Read ReentrancyDemo. AuditedAccount.withdraw calls super.withdraw, which calls canCover. All three are synchronized on the same object.
Predict whether it finishes or hangs, then run it.

code.title: ReentrancyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. */ public class ReentrancyDemo { static class Account { private long balanceCents = 10_000; public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("withdraw: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents; // takes the same lock again } public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) { System.out.println("canCover: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); return balanceCents >= cents; } } static class AuditedAccount extends Account { @Override public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("audit: about to withdraw " + cents); super.withdraw(cents); // and again, through super } } public static void main(String[] args) { new AuditedAccount().withdraw(2_500); System.out.println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held"); } }

alt.title: ReentrancyDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 // A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. open class SavingsAccount { private var balanceCents = 10_000L @Synchronized open fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("withdraw: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents // takes the same lock again } @Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean { println("canCover: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") return balanceCents >= cents } } class AuditedSavingsAccount : SavingsAccount() { @Synchronized override fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("audit: about to withdraw $cents") super.withdraw(cents) // and again, through super } } fun main() { AuditedSavingsAccount().withdraw(2_500) println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held") }

try.expect: It prints holds the lock? true at each level and finishes. One thread entered one monitor three deep, and the hold count went 1, 2, 3 and back to 0.

sections.h: Choosing the key: lock on a private final object
sections.html:
A lock protects state only if every thread that touches the state uses the same lock, and no unrelated code uses that lock for something else. The safest choice is the boring one:

Java
private final Object lock = new Object();
Kotlin
private val lock = Any()

The lock is private, so no other class can take it and stall you. It's final (a val in Kotlin), so it never changes under you. The other choices go wrong in ways that look harmless in a code review.

A boxed number, like synchronized (declines) on an Integer field, is broken twice. declines++ creates a new Integer and points the field at it, so the next thread locks a different object and nothing is excluded.

Small values are also cached and shared: Integer.valueOf(42) returns the same object everywhere in the JVM. javac knows, and prints warning: [synchronization] attempt to synchronize on an instance of a value-based class. The lab's DeclineCounter makes exactly this mistake.

A string literal, like synchronized ("lock"), is shared by design. Literals are interned, so every class in the JVM that writes "lock" gets the same object. In SharedLiteralLock, a token cache and an unrelated metrics class each lock on "lock". While the cache spends a second refreshing, the metrics thread sits BLOCKED. The demo reports that it waited about 900 ms for a lock it never shared on purpose.

A field that isn't final can be reassigned, and then threads before and after the change lock different objects.

this on a public class works, and a synchronized method does exactly that. But any caller can also write synchronized (account) { ... } and hold your key for as long as it likes. A private lock keeps that decision inside your class.

synchronized (new Object()) is always wrong. Every thread locks its own fresh object, so nobody ever waits and nobody is promised anything. It's a lock that protects nothing.

The opposite mistake is two keys for one piece of state. The classic case is a static field updated in a synchronized instance method. Each instance locks itself, so two instances update the shared field at the same time. The worked example below fixes one.

Give each piece of state one private final lock. Take it everywhere the state is touched.

The key is right now, and every reader takes it. A good lock can still make a service slow, though. It depends on what runs while the key is held.

try.title: Share a lock by accident
steps: Read SharedLiteralLock. TokenCache and Metrics never mention each other, and each one locks on "lock".
Predict the metrics thread's state after 200 ms, then run it and read how long it waited.
In the lab you'll compile DeclineCounter, which locks on an Integer. Look for javac's [synchronization] warning in the Gradle output when you do.

code.title: SharedLiteralLock.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. */ public class SharedLiteralLock { static class TokenCache { void refresh() { synchronized ("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. sleep(1_000); // a slow refresh } } } static class Metrics { void record() { synchronized ("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? System.out.println("metrics: recorded"); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> new TokenCache().refresh(), "token-refresh"); Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> new Metrics().record(), "metrics"); refresher.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the refresher take the lock first long t0 = System.nanoTime(); metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: " + metrics.getState()); metrics.join(); System.out.printf("metrics waited about %d ms for a lock it never shared on purpose%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); refresher.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: SharedLiteralLock.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 // Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. private class TokenCache { fun refresh() { synchronized("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. Thread.sleep(1_000) // a slow refresh } } } private class Metrics { fun record() { synchronized("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? println("metrics: recorded") } } } fun main() { val refresher = Thread({ TokenCache().refresh() }, "token-refresh") val metrics = Thread({ Metrics().record() }, "metrics") refresher.start() Thread.sleep(100) // let the refresher take the lock first val t0 = System.nanoTime() metrics.start() Thread.sleep(200) println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: ${metrics.state}") metrics.join() println("metrics waited about ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms for a lock it never shared on purpose") refresher.join() }

try.expect: The metrics thread is BLOCKED after 200 ms, and it waits about 900 ms in all, the rest of the token refresh. Two classes that never mention each other contend on one lock, because both literals are the same interned String.

sections.h: Keeping slow calls and alien code out of the lock
sections.html:
Everything inside a synchronized block runs one thread at a time, so anything slow in there turns your thread pool into a queue of one. SlowCallUnderLock makes that concrete. Eight threads each authorize five payments, and each call to the card issuer takes 40 ms. Both versions update approvedCents under the lock, and only one of them also holds the lock during the call.

My guess before running it: with the call inside the lock, the 40 calls run one after another, about 1,600 ms. With the call outside, they overlap in 5 rounds of 8, about 200 ms. It printed:

issuer call inside the lock:  1,618 ms
issuer call outside the lock:   201 ms

The guess held, and both versions got the total right (the demo checks it). With the call inside the lock, eight threads, forty calls and one key made a very orderly queue. The card issuer takes its 40 ms either way. The only question is whether everyone else waits while it does.

So put only the reads and writes of shared state inside the lock. Do the I/O, the parsing and the computing before it or after it.

A worse form of the same mistake is calling alien code while you hold a lock. Alien code is code you don't control: a listener, a callback, a method a subclass can override, a lambda someone passed in. It might make a 2-second HTTP call.

Alien code might also hand work to another thread and wait for it, and if that thread needs your lock, the two wait for each other forever. That's a deadlock, the subject of lesson 6 of this track. Or it might call back into your object on the same thread, where reentrancy lets it in halfway through your update.

The JDK has shipped this bug itself. JDK 25 carries a fix titled "j.u.l.Handler classes create deadlock risk via synchronized publish() method".

The fix has the same shape every time. Under the lock, change your own state and take a copy of what you need. Release the lock. Then call out.

Both versions copy the listeners under the lock and notify them outside it:

Java
List<Listener> toNotify;
synchronized (lock) {
    rates.put(pair, rate);               // 1. our state, under the lock
    toNotify = List.copyOf(listeners);   // 2. a snapshot to work from
}
for (Listener l : toNotify) l.onRate(pair, rate);   // 3. alien code, no lock held
Kotlin
val toNotify = synchronized(lock) {
    rates[pair] = rate                   // 1. our state, under the lock
    listeners.toList()                   // 2. a snapshot to work from (the block's value)
}
for (l in toNotify) l.onRate(pair, rate) // 3. alien code, no lock held

The Kotlin version is one variable shorter, because synchronized is a function and returns its block's value. The cost of the pattern is small: a listener may hear about two rates in a different order than two threads published them. That's almost always a price worth paying.

Hold a lock only for your own reads and writes. Call out after you let go.

That's the whole toolkit of this lesson, so let's be honest about where it stops. Our ledger has one lock for every balance, so two transfers between four different accounts still wait for each other.

Give each account its own lock and a transfer must hold two, which is how lesson 6 of this track gets its deadlock. And a transfer that finds too little money can only refuse. While it holds the key, it can't wait for a deposit, because the deposit needs the key too.

try.title: Move the slow call out of the lock
steps: Read SlowCallUnderLock. Both versions update approvedCents under the lock. Only one also holds the lock during the 40 ms issuer call.
Predict both times (8 threads x 5 calls x 40 ms), then run it.

code.title: SlowCallUnderLock.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Eight threads authorize payments. Each call to the issuer takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? */ public class SlowCallUnderLock { static final Object lock = new Object(); static long approvedCents; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("issuer call inside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(true)); System.out.printf("issuer call outside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(false)); } static long run(boolean callInsideLock) throws InterruptedException { approvedCents = 0; Thread[] threads = new Thread[8]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) { threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < 5; p++) { if (callInsideLock) { synchronized (lock) { boolean ok = callIssuer(); // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999; } } else { boolean ok = callIssuer(); // slow work with no lock held synchronized (lock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999; } } } }); threads[i].start(); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); if (approvedCents != 40 * 1_999) throw new AssertionError("lost an update: " + approvedCents); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static boolean callIssuer() { try { Thread.sleep(40); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return true; } }

alt.title: SlowCallUnderLock.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads authorize payments. Each call to the issuer takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? private val issuerLock = Any() private var approvedCents = 0L // guarded by issuerLock fun main() { println("issuer call inside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(callInsideLock = true))) println("issuer call outside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(callInsideLock = false))) } private fun run(callInsideLock: Boolean): Long { approvedCents = 0 val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(8) { thread { repeat(5) { if (callInsideLock) { synchronized(issuerLock) { val ok = callIssuer() // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999 } } else { val ok = callIssuer() // slow work with no lock held synchronized(issuerLock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999 } } } } } threads.forEach { it.join() } check(approvedCents == 40L * 1_999) { "lost an update: $approvedCents" } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } private fun callIssuer(): Boolean { Thread.sleep(40) return true }

try.expect: About 1,600 ms with the call inside the lock (40 calls in a row) and about 200 ms with it outside (5 rounds of 8 calls at once). Both versions get the total right. Only one of them can serve traffic.

compare.title: Locking in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: public class DeclineCounter { private final Object lock = new Object(); private int declines; public void recordDecline() { synchronized (lock) { // a keyword declines++; } } public int total() { synchronized (lock) { return declines; } } } public class HitCounter { private int hits; public synchronized void hit() { hits++; } // locks this public synchronized int total() { return hits; } }

kotlin.title: KotlinLocks.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l04 class DeclineCounterKt { private val lock = Any() // a private lock object, like `new Object()` in Java private var declines = 0 fun recordDecline() { synchronized(lock) { // a standard-library function, not a keyword declines++ } } fun total(): Int = synchronized(lock) { declines } // it returns the block's value } class HitCounterKt { private var hits = 0 @Synchronized fun hit() { hits++ } // like a Java synchronized method: locks `this` @Synchronized fun total() = hits } fun main() { val declines = DeclineCounterKt() val hits = HitCounterKt() val threads = List(8) { Thread { repeat(100_000) { declines.recordDecline() hits.hit() } }.apply { start() } } threads.forEach { it.join() } println("declines = ${declines.total()}, hits = ${hits.total()}") }

compare.note: Both files lock the same way and compile to the same monitor instructions. Three things differ. Kotlin has no synchronized keyword: synchronized(lock) { ... } is an inline standard-library function, and the compiler emits the same monitorenter and monitorexit as a Java block. Because it's a function, it returns its block's value, so total() is one expression. And @Synchronized on a function marks the compiled method as synchronized, exactly like Java's modifier, so it locks this (or, in an object, the object itself). Any() makes a fine private lock. One gap shows up in the next lesson: Any has no wait() or notify(), so Kotlin code that needs them locks on a java.lang.Object or, better, uses the explicit locks from lesson 7 of this track.

worked.title: Fix a refund limiter with the wrong lock and a slow call inside

steps.say: A refund service caps the total refunded per process. It runs as two bean instances behind a router. Find every lock problem before you read on.
steps.code: public class RefundLimiter { private static long refundedCents; // shared by every instance private static final long LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000; public synchronized boolean tryRefund(long cents) { // locks `this` if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents); // HTTP call, about 300 ms refundedCents += cents; return true; } }

alt.html: class RefundLimiter { companion object { private var refundedCents = 0L // shared by every instance private const val LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000L } @Synchronized fun tryRefund(cents: Long): Boolean { // locks `this` if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents) // HTTP call, about 300 ms refundedCents += cents return true } }

steps.say: There are two problems. First, the method locks this, but the state is static: two keys for one piece of state. Two instances lock two different monitors and can both pass the limit check at once. Second, a 300 ms HTTP call runs while the key is held, so every refund waits for the previous one's call. Fix the lock first: one lock object for the one piece of state.
steps.code: private static final Object LOCK = new Object(); // 1. one lock for the static state

alt.html: private val LOCK = Any() // 1. one lock for the shared state, in the companion object

steps.say: Now shrink the critical section. Reserve the amount under the lock, so the check and the update are one step. Then release the lock and make the call. If the call fails and the refund should not go ahead, give the reservation back, under the lock again. Before you read the last step, ask yourself why the check and the += must stay inside the same block.
steps.code: public boolean tryRefund(long cents) { synchronized (LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; refundedCents += cents; } try { riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents); // 3. slow call, no lock held return true; } catch (RuntimeException e) { synchronized (LOCK) { refundedCents -= cents; } // 4. undo the reservation throw e; } }

alt.html: fun tryRefund(cents: Long): Boolean { synchronized(LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false refundedCents += cents } try { riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents) // 3. slow call, no lock held return true } catch (e: RuntimeException) { synchronized(LOCK) { refundedCents -= cents } // 4. undo the reservation throw e } }

steps.say: Split the check from the += and you're back in Race conditions: why count++ lies, with check-then-act and two threads that both pass the check. The lock has to cover the whole compound action. What it must not cover is the 300 ms call, and now it doesn't. If the limit must hold across pods, the reservation belongs in the database, but the shape stays the same.

lab.title: Pick the right lock, then get alien code out of it
steps: Run the tests. Three of the four fail. The fourth checks that listeners still hear every rate, so keep it green while you fix the others. Look for the [synchronization] warning that javac prints for DeclineCounter.
Fix DeclineCounter: lock on a private final Object and keep the count in a plain int. Guard total() with the same lock.

Read the two FxRateBoard failures. In one, a listener waits for another thread to read the board. In the other, a listener subscribes a new listener and hits ConcurrentModificationException, the reentrancy side effect from the second section.
Fix FxRateBoard.publish: update the map and copy the listener list under the lock, then notify the copy with no lock held.
Run the tests until all four pass, then run them twice more.
hints: declines++ on an Integer field is declines = Integer.valueOf(declines.intValue() + 1). Which object does the next thread lock?
List.copyOf(listeners) gives you an immutable snapshot. A listener that subscribes during the loop changes the real list, not the copy you're iterating.
The cross-thread test fails after 2 seconds rather than hanging: the listener gives up waiting for its helper. If it fails, your listener is still being called while lock is held.
lab.done: All four tests in SynchronizedTest pass, three runs in a row, and the [synchronization] warning is gone.

drill.title: Copy under the lock, call outside it
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class StatusBoard with a String status, a list of Consumer<String> listeners, subscribe(listener) and update(newStatus). update must store the status and notify every listener, without ever calling a listener while it holds the lock.

answer.html: public class StatusBoard { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final List<Consumer<String>> listeners = new ArrayList<>(); private String status; public void subscribe(Consumer<String> l) { synchronized (lock) { listeners.add(l); } } public void update(String newStatus) { List<Consumer<String>> toNotify; synchronized (lock) { status = newStatus; toNotify = List.copyOf(listeners); } for (Consumer<String> l : toNotify) l.accept(newStatus); } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class StatusBoard { private val lock = Any() private val listeners = mutableListOf<(String) -> Unit>() private var status: String? = null fun subscribe(l: (String) -> Unit) { synchronized(lock) { listeners += l } } fun update(newStatus: String) { val toNotify = synchronized(lock) { status = newStatus listeners.toList() } for (l in toNotify) l(newStatus) } }

recap: synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility, but only between threads that use the same monitor. Readers need the lock too.
A synchronized instance method locks this, a static one locks the Class object, and a block locks the object you name.
Monitors are reentrant: the thread that holds one can enter it again, which also lets a callback on that thread back in mid-update.
Lock on a private final Object, one lock per piece of state. Never on boxed numbers, string literals, non-final fields or new Object().
Keep only shared-state reads and writes inside the lock. Copy what you need, release it, then do I/O or call alien code.
The limit: one lock serializes everything it guards, two locks can deadlock, and a thread holding a lock can't wait for another thread to change the state.

explain.prompt: A colleague's PR adds synchronized to a publish() method that loops over listeners, "to make it thread-safe". Explain what can go wrong with that, and what you would suggest instead.
explain.answer: Making publish() synchronized protects the board's own state, but it also means every listener now runs while the lock is held. A slow listener makes every other thread that needs the board wait. A listener that hands work to another thread and waits for it can deadlock, because that thread may need the same lock. And because the lock is reentrant, a listener that calls back into the board on the same thread gets straight in, for example adding a listener while we iterate, which throws ConcurrentModificationException. I'd keep the lock only around updating the map and copying the listener list, then release it and notify the copy.

deeper.html:
How does HotSpot make synchronized cheap when nobody else wants the lock? It doesn't build a full monitor object for every lock. An uncontended lock is a small change in the object's header (lightweight locking). Only when threads really fight over it, or one calls wait(), does the JVM inflate it into a full ObjectMonitor, with an entry queue and a wait set.

The details keep changing between releases, which is a good reason not to depend on them. Lightweight locking became the default LockingMode in JDK 23, the option was deprecated in JDK 24, and its code was removed in JDK 26. JDK 27 switched on, by default, a separate table that maps objects to their monitors, and made compact object headers the default too. None of this changes what synchronized means. It only changes what it costs.

If you want to see contention rather than guess at it, Java Flight Recorder records a jdk.JavaMonitorEnter event when a thread has to wait for a monitor, with the monitor's class and the previous owner. JDK 25 added jdk.JavaMonitorNotify and jdk.JavaMonitorStatistics. Lesson 13 of this track uses them.

For virtual threads, JEP 491 in JDK 24 is the change to know. Before it, a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized held on to its carrier thread. Since JDK 24 it doesn't, in most cases.
